executive_summary: SGD/JPY closed at 123.267 on 30 October 2026. The pair is quoted in yen per Singapore dollar, so a rising quote means a stronger Singapore dollar. It fell 0.16% over one month, rose 0.20% over three months, fell 0.33% over six months and rose 3.73% over a year, and it sits at the 61st percentile of its 52-week closing range of 117.44-126.96. Both legs of the cross are policy-managed. The S$NEER band damps USD/SGD, and the Ministry of Finance caps USD/JPY. As a result, the pair's two largest moves of the past six months came from yen-leg policy shocks: a 3.2% fall over the 30-31 July intervention and a 3.7% slide from 2 to 11 September. The bilateral story sets Singapore's 5.4% growth, a current account surplus near 17% of GDP and an AAA balance sheet against Japan's energy-driven trade deficits, with JKM LNG up 27% in October and five straight monthly shortfalls, and against a debt-financed tax cut. Weighing the other way, Bank of Japan guidance is the only policy channel active in the window, and it leans hawkish. Some differentials only show up at the pair level. The short-rate gap is just 5bp, so carry does not drive the pair. Spot is only 0.4% above the shared PPP estimate of 122.75, so valuation is neutral. And a forward built from the two dollar legs pays a Singapore dollar long about 0.46% a year. The tactical stance is Bullish at conviction 2 (score +0.118), with a base case of 124.00 by 27 November, an entry inside the five-touch support band at 122.95-123.25 and a stop below 122.20. The strategic stance is Neutral at conviction 1 (score +0.021), with a base case of 123.00 by end-April 2027, almost exactly on the 122.98 six-month forward built the same way. The caveat is that spot sits below all three daily moving averages and has made lower highs since 24 September, and strategists report the Singapore dollar being taken up as a carry-funding rival to the yen. Both of those lean against the tactical call, so it should stay small and short-dated and be cut ahead of the 18 December BoJ meeting.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Bilateral valuation is close to fair, in sharp contrast with each currency's standalone valuation. Both dossiers' World Bank PPP calculations put fair SGD/JPY at about 122.75 (flagged as best available), so spot at 123.267 is only 0.4% above PPP. Trade-weighted, the two currencies sit at opposite extremes. The BIS real effective rate for the Singapore dollar is 115.04, at the 88th percentile of its range since January 2024. The yen's is 66.61, at about the 21st percentile and the lowest in G10+SGD by 26.8 points. The yen is extremely cheap against the dollar, the euro and the franc, but not against the Singapore dollar, because Singapore's measured price level is also low relative to its income. The current level therefore prices no valuation premium either way. Mean reversion in the yen's trade-weighted value would mostly show up in EUR/JPY, CHF/JPY and USD/JPY rather than in this cross. Valuation provides no edge on either horizon.

positioning.net_pair_implication: Netting the two, a crowded yen long against a moderately long Singapore dollar tilts squeeze risk towards a higher SGD/JPY. If carry funders move from yen to Singapore dollars, they buy back yen and sell Singapore dollars, which pushes SGD/JPY lower at the margin. That is a structural headwind to the tactical call; its size is unmeasurable for now, so it is a risk to monitor rather than a scored input.

market_context.recent_regime: The cross has spent the last three months recovering from two yen-policy shocks: the joint US-Japan intervention at the end of July and the US Treasury's anti-reflation message in early September. Since mid-September it has traded a compressing 122.3-124.2 range. The dominant narrative is a contest between Japan's energy bill and stagnant growth, which weaken the yen, and a BoJ that judged underlying inflation 'generally consistent with' 2% on 30 October, which supports it. MAS's 14 October hold took the hawkish impulse out of the Singapore side and made the BoJ the only policy engine. Over October the cross slipped because the yen firmed while USD/SGD stood still. A note built from MAS fixing data showed the cross implied by the MAS fix falling to 122.83 on 23 October from 123.61 on 1 October, while the Singapore dollar barely moved against the US dollar, from 1.2792 to 1.2775.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The short-rate carry is +4.7bp a year: three-month compounded SORA at 1.297% (30 October) against the BoJ call rate of 1.25%. That is the smallest absolute carry of any SGD or JPY cross, and a 25bp BoJ hike on 18 December would turn it to about -20bp. No quoted forward or futures-based funding differential exists for this pair, so a forward is built from the dossiers' two dollar-leg forwards (ING indicative USD/SGD points of 12 October applied to 1.27819; CME yen futures roll of 29 October). The resulting SGD/JPY forwards are 123.15 at one month (-11 pips), 123.08 at three months (-19 pips) and 122.98 at six months (-28 pips), which puts the Singapore dollar as the higher forward-implied yielder at about +0.61% annualised at three months and +0.46% (about +46bp) at six; the one-month figure (+1.1%) is noisy because the two sources were observed on different dates. The gap to the 5bp cash differential comes from the yen's negative cross-currency basis and expected BoJ tightening, embedded in the CME roll's roughly 25bp excess yen forward premium. No pair implied volatility exists, so the standard carry-to-vol ratio cannot be formed; against 60-day realised volatility of 6.21% the ratio is 0.008 on the short-rate basis and 0.07 on the forward basis. Even the forward-basis figure is worth about 6 pips a month, a tenth of one day's ATR, so carry is not a driver.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Singapore has no policy rate. MAS steers the S$NEER inside an undisclosed band and left the slope, width and centre unchanged on 14 October. The bilateral comparison therefore uses three-month compounded SORA, 1.297% on 30 October, against the Bank of Japan's call rate of 1.25%. That leaves a short-rate gap of only about 5bp in the Singapore dollar's favour. At ten years the gap runs the other way: the SGS 10-year closed at 2.24% on 30 October against 2.770% on the JGB 10-year the same day, about 53bp in the yen's favour. That long-end gap comes from Japan's fiscal term premium rather than from policy. The next Bank of Japan decision is 18 December, after the four-week window closes, and no verified MAS decision date is on file inside the window, so neither leg's policy setting can change before late November. Carry of about 5bp a year is economically irrelevant for this cross, so the pair does not attract the carry-funded positioning that drives yen crosses such as AUD/JPY. Tactically the factor is Neutral: the differential is flat and no scheduled event can move it within four weeks. The communication channel that could shift December pricing is scored under Guidance.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over the strategic horizon the short-rate gap turns modestly in the yen's favour. A 25bp BoJ hike on 18 December would take it from about +5bp to about -20bp, and a second hike, which the yen dossier places around April, would leave it near -45bp. MAS is expected to hold its band: the Singapore-side probabilities for January are 75% hold, 15% slight slope increase and 10% reduction. SORA is not fixed, though. It follows US rates with a lag and has risen from a 1.06% second-quarter average to about 1.30%, so a December Fed hike would partly offset BoJ tightening in the bilateral gap. The BoJ leg is also already in the curve. Twelve-month swaps take the call rate towards about 2.00%, and the yen dossier's own December probability of 65% sits below the roughly 75% priced, so the risk on 18 December is at least as much a hawkish disappointment as a hawkish surprise. The 22 January meeting carries an Outlook Report and is the scheduled point at which a second hike would be signalled. MAS's appreciating slope steadily lifts the trade-weighted Singapore dollar, which includes the yen, but the slope is unchanged and priced. Strategically the factor is Neutral: the differential is moving towards the yen, but the move is small, already priced, and the surprise risk around 18 December cuts both ways.

Breakeven: an SGD/JPY long earns roughly 0.05% of spot a year, so almost any adverse move erases it within days; after a December BoJ hike the sign reverses and holding the long costs about 0.2% a year, still trivial against normal pair moves.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Singapore is growing far faster than Japan. Third-quarter GDP rose 5.4% y/y and 1.1% q/q, and September non-oil domestic exports rose 68.4%. Japan grew 0.73% y/y, the JCER consensus for third-quarter GDP on 16 November is only +0.08% annualised, and the yen dossier puts the chance of a negative print at 40%. Inflation is close: MAS core inflation was 2.0% in September, against 2.1% for Japan's CPI excluding fresh food and 2.4% excluding fresh food and energy. Tokyo's October reading of 2.6% points to a national print of 2.3-2.5% on 20 November. The two legs react to data differently. Singapore surprises are absorbed by the band and rarely move MAS within a quarter, whereas Japanese releases move December BoJ pricing directly, so the yen leg carries most of the pair's data sensitivity. Japan's two releases in the window point in opposite directions. The growth print is the less priced of the two, because the market treats December as if growth were firm, while CPI strength has already been flagged by Tokyo. Singapore's run of positive surprises keeps the S$NEER in the upper half of its band and removes any easing risk. We lean Bullish with low confidence: the growth gap is wide, and the less-priced Japanese release in the window carries downside risk for the yen.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months, inflation and wages matter more than the growth gap, because they decide which central bank changes policy. Japan's Outlook Report raised FY2027 core CPI to 2.6%. Firms' Tankan price expectations sit at 2.5-2.6%, and the 2026 Shunto settled at 5.01%, a profile that supports further BoJ normalisation; the first tally of the 2027 wage round is due in March. Singapore's profile points the other way for policy. MAS expects the positive output gap to narrow through 2027 and core inflation to ease noticeably from mid-2027. NODX growth will also slow as the AI export surge runs into a high base, which leaves the band unchanged. Growth still favours Singapore by a wide margin. But under an exchange-rate target, growth only tightens policy if inflation follows, so it is a weaker currency driver than Japan's inflation turn. The main risk to this reading is Japan's food consumption-tax cut from April 2027: it mechanically lowers measured CPI and could be read dovishly. Japan's weak potential growth of about 0.5% is a second risk. Strategically the factor is Bearish at low confidence: Japan's data are moving its policy, while Singapore's are holding its policy still.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Neither leg is a high-beta risk currency. The Singapore dollar is a low-beta currency of a AAA financial hub, managed inside a band. The yen is a haven whose response in this cycle has been muted by the energy shock. That puts SGD/JPY in the low-to-moderate risk-sensitivity group rather than among the risk-proxy crosses. The risk channel that matters is the AI equity trade. The Nikkei fell 8.22% in October to about 63,290, 13% below its June record, US high-yield spreads widened 18bp in a month to 326bp, and VIX traded at 20.05 intraday on 30 October. An AI-led correction hits Singapore harder than a generic sell-off, because electronics drove the 107.6% jump in September NODX. The same shock tends to pull Japanese investors back home and strengthen the yen. The other large tail, a US strike on Iran after the midterms, would lift oil and hurt the yen more than the Singapore dollar, but that channel is scored under External Balance and Event Risk rather than here. On risk appetite alone, the marginal deterioration favours the yen, so we lean Bearish at low confidence.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months the risk channel is two-sided for this cross, because the cycle's main shock is an energy war rather than a financial crisis. In the escalation phase the yen weakened against the dollar and only intervention reversed it, so the classic haven bid was overwhelmed by the terms-of-trade loss. The Singapore dollar, cushioned by its band and its refining sector, held up better. A Gulf settlement would bring risk-on and lower oil at the same time. That helps the yen through its trade balance and helps the Singapore dollar through Asian growth and capital flows, so the effects largely cancel in the cross. An AI investment pullback, which MAS lists as a downside growth risk, would hit Singapore's export engine and Japanese equities together, and Japanese repatriation would give the yen the edge. China's stable 4.5% growth removes the regional-contagion channel that historically pushes haven flows into Singapore. Strategically the factor is Neutral: the outcomes are spread wide, but their net effect on this pair is small and close to symmetric.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both legs carry long positioning, but only the yen's is measured and stretched. CFTC data for the week to 27 October show asset managers net long 91,191 yen contracts, the largest of 25 weeks. The legacy non-commercial net long jumped to 101,600 from 69,900, beyond the +80,000 level that has marked stretched yen longs in past cycles. That length was built against the dollar into a month with no BoJ meeting, so a liquidation would push the yen lower against every currency, including the Singapore dollar. The Singapore dollar has no reportable futures contract. Its proxy is the S$NEER at about 1.65% above the band mid-point on 15 October, which leaves more room to slip than to rise, and MAS reserve accumulation of S$2.84bn in September shows smoothing of strength. Netting the two: the Singapore dollar's trade-weighted length is moderate and is trimmed only gradually, because the band's rising mid-point absorbs it. The yen's speculative length is extreme and exposed to identifiable triggers in the window. The combined signal therefore favours SGD/JPY at the margin, at low confidence, because the Singapore dollar side is inferred rather than observed.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Both economies import energy, but Japan's exposure to LNG and crude is far larger and is the sharpest bilateral asymmetry between the two currencies, so the factor is raised by 0.03 on both horizons.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The external-balance gap is wide and widening in the Singapore dollar's favour. Singapore's current account surplus was 16.7% of GDP in 2025, and the second-quarter surplus of S$37.08bn was 21% higher than a year earlier, driven by an AI export boom. Japan's current account is 5.03% of GDP, but its trade balance has been in deficit for five months. The September deficit of JPY536.6bn was almost three times the forecast, as crude imports rose 51.1%. Both are energy importers, but the transmission differs. JKM LNG rose 27.4% in October to $32.84/MMBtu, a direct hit to Japan's import bill. Singapore partly offsets higher oil through refining and re-export margins. Japan's primary-income surplus is largely reinvested abroad rather than converted into yen, so it does not cushion the currency. Bilaterally, IMF DOTS shows Singapore exporting $17.8bn of goods to Japan in 2024 and importing $22.2bn, a $4.5bn deficit for Singapore. That is small relative to either economy and does not create a meaningful pair-specific flow. Strategically the factor is Bullish at moderate confidence and carries the largest weight in the score.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: SGD: net crude importer, but a large refining and bunkering hub, so higher oil raises the import bill while lifting refining margins. Classed among currencies that lose mildly when oil rises (Oil up -> -SGD; LNG/JKM up -> -SGD). The dominant export engine is electronics, not commodities.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: JPY: heavy importer of crude and LNG with no domestic offset (Oil up -> --JPY; LNG/JKM up -> --JPY). The trade balance has been in deficit for five months on energy.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Applying the direction rules: oil up gives SGD a mild negative (-) and JPY a strong negative (--), so the net effect is pair up. JKM LNG up gives SGD a mild negative (-) and JPY a strong negative (--), so the net effect is pair up again. Gold is not a driver for either leg. Iron ore and dairy are irrelevant. Netting the energy complex: both legs lose when energy rises, but Japan loses roughly twice as much because it has no refining offset and imports LNG at scale. The energy exposure is therefore net long SGD/JPY, rising when energy rises and falling when it falls.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: A 10% rise in oil, with JKM following, widens Japan's monthly import bill by roughly JPY0.3-0.4tn on the yen dossier's estimate, while Singapore's refining margins partly offset its higher bill. Net impact: SGD/JPY higher.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: A 10% fall in oil narrows Japan's deficit more than it helps Singapore, removing part of the yen's energy discount. Net impact: SGD/JPY lower.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: JKM LNG, through Japan's import bill, is the dominant commodity driver for this pair, with Brent second.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: The two central banks run very different communication regimes: one reprices through scheduled meetings and commentary, the other speaks quarterly and does not disclose its band. BoJ guidance is therefore the main policy-repricing channel for this cross, so the factor is raised by 0.02 on both horizons.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Guidance is lopsided. The BoJ's 30 October hold was hawkish: its View moved underlying inflation from 'approaching' 2% to 'at a level generally consistent with' 2%, it said it will continue to raise rates, and Takata dissented in favour of 1.50%. Ueda added that the Bank must be vigilant to the risk of inflation overshooting. The Bank has communication events inside the window: Ueda's remarks on 6 November and the Summary of Opinions in the second week of November. The yen dossier judges December pricing of about 75% to sit slightly below what the language implies. MAS last spoke on 14 October with a hawkish hold, saying risks to inflation remain tilted to the upside. It has no scheduled communication before its January statement, for which no verified date is on file. MAS credibility is very high, but its guidance cannot change inside four weeks. The Ministry of Finance adds a second, one-directional channel: renewed warnings about yen weakness against the dollar would lift the yen against all currencies. Tactically the factor is Bearish: the only active guidance in the window comes from the yen side and leans hawkish relative to pricing.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are credible and both lean hawkish, but only one is actively moving. The BoJ hiked in December 2025, June 2026 and September 2026 as telegraphed. Its voting has shifted from a 7-2 hike with two dovish dissents in September to an 8-1 hold with a hawkish dissent in October, and it has two decisions on file in the window: 18 December and 22 January, the latter with an Outlook Report. MAS's guidance carries an asymmetric tightening bias, with Singapore-side odds of 15% for a slight slope increase against 10% for a reduction. Its central case is an extended hold, and MAS itself expects core inflation to ease from mid-2027. The appreciating slope is a durable support for the trade-weighted Singapore dollar, but it is a constant rather than a change. On credibility, the Ministry of Finance's two intervention episodes in 2026, one coordinated with the US Treasury, make yen weakness against the dollar a policy-capped outcome, which also limits how far the yen can fall against the Singapore dollar. Strategically the factor is Bearish at low confidence: the yen side's guidance points to further tightening at scheduled dates, while the Singapore side points to a hold.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The binary events in the window are mostly external and pull this cross in opposite directions. A US strike on Iran after the 3 November midterms would lift oil and LNG, hurting the yen through its energy bill more than the Singapore dollar, and push the pair higher. Two tankers were hit in the Strait of Hormuz in 24 hours at the end of October. Yen intervention by the Ministry of Finance is the opposite tail: it would be triggered by dollar strength against the yen and would lift the yen against all currencies, including the Singapore dollar. The yen dossier puts a test of the intervention line at 20% within four weeks and intervention, if tested, at 60%. The 10-year JGB auction on 5 November is a domestic fiscal test that could weaken the yen if it tails. Singapore's domestic political risk is negligible and no Singapore event is scheduled. No bilateral political or trade dispute exists between the two economies. With an escalation tail that lifts the pair and an intervention tail that lowers it, of similar size and probability, the factor is Neutral.

Both economies sit in the US-China technology supply chain, so export-control escalation would affect them in a broadly similar way. Strategically the factor is Neutral: the tails are wide, but they point in opposite directions for this pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal gap is among the widest of any pair. Singapore is rated AAA by all three agencies, ran a FY2025 surplus of S$15.1bn (1.9% of GDP) and projects a further surplus in FY2026, with past reserves contributing 17.4% of revenue. Japan's gross debt is above 230% of GDP and FY2026 debt service exceeds JPY31tn. The Takaichi government plans to cut the food consumption tax from 8% to 1% from April 2027, and the Prime Minister said on 19 October that additional JGB issuance has not been ruled out. The bond market has already charged for this: the 10-year JGB reached 3.135% on 7 October, the highest since 1996, before falling back to 2.770% by 30 October. The 5 November 10-year auction is the only fiscal test in the window. A weak result would revive the term-premium story, and in this cycle higher JGB yields on supply have weakened the yen rather than strengthened it. The factor is Bullish for the pair at low weight.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over six months Japan's fiscal risk becomes live, because the FY2027 draft budget due by year-end will quantify the tax cut and cash payments for the first time. Oxford Economics estimates the tax cut at about JPY5tn a year, half debt-financed, with a primary deficit near 3% of GDP in 2027-2028 and the 10-year JGB near 3% by end-2026. The BoJ is tapering its JGB purchases at the same time, so the market must absorb more duration as issuance rises. That is the pattern in which a higher term premium and a weaker currency arrive together. Singapore faces nothing comparable. Its FY2027 Budget, expected in February, is likely to stay in surplus, and the reserves backing it also back the currency. Mitigants on the Japanese side are real: domestic institutions hold most JGBs, Fitch expects deficits to stay manageable, and ratings are stable. Strategically the factor is Bullish at moderate confidence and low weight.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: SGD/JPY is a thin cross. It is priced and executed through its two dollar legs, and each leg is managed. USD/SGD trades inside an S$NEER band that damps its moves, and USD/JPY trades under a Ministry of Finance ceiling that has been defended twice this year. The cross's volatility therefore comes mostly from the yen leg. Its distribution is shaped by policy: yen weakness against the dollar is truncated by intervention risk, while yen strength on risk-off or BoJ repricing is open. No implied volatility, risk reversal or vol surface exists for this pair, because the Singapore dollar has no listed FX option on any exchange. The only observable option market is CME's yen contract against the dollar. There, one-month implied volatility of 7.16% sits at about the 19th percentile of its short history, and the risk reversal charges a premium for yen weakness. We do not assess this pair's own chart here; price levels are set in the trade plan below. On structure alone the factor is Neutral.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar liquidity is tightening at the margin through Fed policy rather than funding stress. The Fed held at 3.75-4.00% on 28 October with two dissents for a hike, SOFR was 3.94% on 29 October, and swap-line usage is only $170m. A December Fed hike is priced at roughly 68-77% depending on the source. For this cross, dollar firmness has two opposing effects. The Singapore dollar's band damps its beta to the dollar, while the yen's beta is higher, so a firmer dollar tends to weaken the yen more than the Singapore dollar and lift the pair. Against that, Japanese investors face hedged US Treasury yields below JGB yields, which encourages repatriation, and the intervention ceiling truncates yen weakness against the dollar. Year-end dollar demand from late November affects both legs: it widens the yen basis and lifts SORA through Singapore's role as an Asian dollar hub. Tactically the factor is Neutral: the channels offset and no figure points clearly in either direction.

tactical.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.118 is only just above the +0.10 Bullish threshold. Four factors favour SGD/JPY (growth, positioning, external balance, fiscal) and contribute +0.217. Two favour the yen (risk appetite, guidance) and contribute -0.099. The heaviest factor, Policy & Rates, is Neutral. Breadth rather than depth is doing the work: no single factor contributes more than +0.092, and one change of stance in Growth or Positioning would return the call to Neutral. Mapping to conviction: +0.118 maps to Bullish under the ±0.10 rule, at conviction 2, the bottom of the directional band.
tactical.rationale: At tactical weights, Inflation & Growth (0.18), Positioning (0.10), Risk Appetite (0.10) and the raised External Balance and Guidance weights (0.09 each) decide the score, because Policy & Rates is Neutral. The short-rate gap between three-month SORA and the BoJ call rate is only about 5bp, and neither central bank has a decision inside four weeks. Growth contributes +0.092: Singapore's 5.4% growth and 68.4% export surge contrast with a Japanese third-quarter GDP consensus near zero, and the 16 November print is the least-priced risk to December BoJ pricing. Positioning adds +0.052 because the yen leg carries an extreme speculative long, legacy net +101,600 contracts with asset managers at a 25-week high, against moderate trade-weighted Singapore dollar length. External Balance adds +0.051: JKM LNG up 27% in October and a fifth straight Japanese trade deficit hit the yen roughly twice as hard as the Singapore dollar. Against that, BoJ guidance subtracts 0.048, because the only active communication in the window, Ueda on 6 November and the Summary of Opinions in the second week of November, comes from a hawkish-leaning Bank. Risk appetite subtracts 0.051, because an AI-led equity correction would hurt Singapore's electronics engine while pulling Japanese money home. The two dossiers reinforce this reading: the Singapore dollar ranks 6th and the yen 8th of 11 tactically, so the standalone views already put the Singapore dollar marginally ahead. What is priced is a December BoJ hike at about 75%. Our edge is that weak Japanese growth and the October trade bill can pull that pricing lower before Japanese CPI on 20 November restores it. The path of least resistance is a mild drift in the Singapore dollar's favour, punctuated by yen strength on any hawkish BoJ signal or intervention. Key dates are 3 November (US midterms), 5 November (JGB auction), 6 November (Ueda), 16 November (Japan GDP), 17 November (trade balance) and 20 November (national CPI). No MAS event is verified for the window. Conviction is 2, not higher, because the score barely clears the threshold, the Singapore dollar positioning evidence is indirect, and a single hawkish Summary of Opinions would flip Guidance and Positioning together. It is not 1 because the energy asymmetry and the growth gap are measured, not inferred. Where this analysis would push back on its own tactical call: the stance stands, but it is a fundamentals-led view against an unhelpful tape. Spot is below the 50-, 100- and 200-day averages and has made four lower highs since 24 September. The market has shown it sells the cross on Japanese inflation news, with a 104-pip fall on 22 October. And strategists report carry funders adopting the Singapore dollar in place of the yen, a flow that pushes the cross lower. None of this changes a factor score. All of it argues for a small position, an entry inside the five-touch band rather than on a chase, and exit discipline ahead of the BoJ's 18 December decision.
tactical.g10_relative_ranking: On the dossiers' own tactical rankings the Singapore dollar is 6th of 11 and the yen 8th, so SGD/JPY is a mid-table, low-beta expression of yen underperformance with near-zero carry. Among yen crosses it is less attractive than CAD/JPY or NOK/JPY, where the counterparty gains from energy and earns carry, and less volatile than AUD/JPY. Among SGD crosses it ranks behind short EUR/SGD, which the Singapore dossier identifies as the cleanest tactical expression of Singapore dollar strength.

strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of +0.021 is Neutral, and it is a genuine stalemate between structural forces. The Singapore dollar's external surplus and Japan's energy bill (+0.106) and Singapore's fiscal strength (+0.039) are offset by the BoJ's tightening guidance (-0.073) and Japan's inflation-and-wage dynamics (-0.052). Policy & Rates, the heaviest factor, is Neutral because the BoJ path is already priced. Mapping to conviction: +0.021 lies inside the ±0.10 Neutral band, at conviction 1.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights, Policy & Rates (0.24), External Balance (0.19) and Guidance (0.14) dominate, and they split Neutral, Bullish and Bearish, leaving a net score of +0.021. Policy & Rates is Neutral because the short-rate gap's move from about +5bp towards -45bp after two BoJ hikes is already in the swaps curve. The yen dossier's own 65% December probability sits below the roughly 75% priced, so 18 December carries two-sided surprise risk. External Balance contributes +0.106: winter LNG at around $33 to $34, five straight Japanese trade deficits and a Singapore surplus near 17% of GDP set the clearest bilateral asymmetry in the pair. Fiscal adds +0.039 because Japan's FY2027 budget will quantify a debt-financed tax cut while Singapore stays in surplus. Guidance subtracts 0.073: the BoJ has two scheduled decisions in the window, 18 December and 22 January with an Outlook Report, and a voting pattern moving hawkish, whereas MAS's central case is an extended hold. Inflation & Growth subtracts 0.052 because Japan's 5.01% wage round and 2.6% FY2027 core forecast keep its policy moving, while Singapore's slowdown keeps the band still. The dossiers explain the stalemate. Both currencies are strategically Bullish on their own, with the yen 2nd and the Singapore dollar 3rd of 11, so the cross nets two similar-strength views. What is priced is roughly two BoJ hikes and a fixed MAS band. Our view matches both, so we see no edge in the policy path. The path of least resistance is sideways, with yen strength around the BoJ dates and Singapore dollar strength on energy spikes and around Japan's year-end budget. The swing scenario is a Gulf settlement, which would remove the yen's energy discount and turn the score Bearish. Key dates are 9 December (FOMC), 18 December (BoJ), Japan's budget at year-end and 22 January (BoJ Outlook Report). No MAS decision date is verified on file. Conviction is 1 because the score sits close to zero and rests on offsetting structural factors, each of which could flip on one event.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically the yen ranks 2nd and the Singapore dollar 3rd of 11 in their own dossiers. That makes SGD/JPY one of the least directional crosses available for either currency: it pairs two structurally supported currencies against each other. Better strategic expressions exist on both sides: short CHF/JPY for yen strength with positive carry, and short EUR/SGD for Singapore dollar strength against an energy-hit currency without an intervention backstop.

strategic.path_expectation: The strategic path runs in three phases. From November to mid-December the tactical drift higher towards 124.00 should fade as the 9 December FOMC and the 18 December BoJ meeting approach. A December hike should push the cross back into the five-touch band at 122.66-123.49. Late December and January are the budget-versus-BoJ phase. The FY2027 draft budget is a pair-positive fiscal event, while the 22 January Outlook Report is a pair-negative policy event, so the cross should oscillate between 122.30 and 124.25 with realised volatility rising towards 7% around both. February to April brings Japanese fiscal year-end repatriation and the first Shunto tally in the third week of March. The winter energy bill should hold the pair near 123.00 into the April BoJ meeting. The shape is a range that returns to its centre, with the five-touch band as its pivot. The outcomes that would break it, a Gulf settlement below and a BoJ stall above, are binary rather than gradual.

consensus_divergence.our_tactical_view: Mildly Bullish SGD/JPY over four weeks (score +0.118, conviction 2): Japan's growth and energy data and a stretched yen long modestly outweigh hawkish BoJ communication.
consensus_divergence.our_strategic_view: Neutral SGD/JPY over one to six months (score +0.021, conviction 1): the energy and fiscal asymmetries favouring the Singapore dollar are offset by BoJ tightening guidance and Japan's inflation profile.
consensus_divergence.divergence_direction: Not measurable against a pair consensus. Against the dollar-leg bank forecasts cited in the dossiers, we are less yen-positive.
consensus_divergence.divergence_magnitude: Not measurable: no bank research forecast for SGD/JPY was located, and an absent consensus is recorded as absent rather than inferred.
consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: No bank publishes a forecast for this cross in the research the dossiers cite. The dollar-leg forecasts in those dossiers (ING for USD/SGD; Bloomberg's survey and MUFG for USD/JPY) expect the yen to gain several times more against the dollar than the Singapore dollar over six months, which implies a lower cross. We weigh Japan's energy bill and its year-end fiscal expansion more heavily than those linear yen paths do. Both forecast sets were also struck before or around central bank decisions that changed the picture: MAS's hold on 14 October and the BoJ's hawkish hold on 30 October. Deriving a cross consensus from two dollar-leg surveys would be a synthetic number, not bank research, so we do not publish one. The pair-specific views that do exist are model outputs or retail commentary, not bank research, and they spread widely: one statistical model projects 127.36 by end-2026, a Singapore retail guide expects the 120-125 range to hold, and a note built from MAS fixing data had a base case of 122.45 by 30 October (bull 123.61, bear 122.06) against a close of 123.267.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: If the energy and fiscal asymmetries persist through the winter, the cross avoids the yen appreciation that combined dollar-leg forecasts imply, and a neutral-to-long Singapore dollar stance outperforms a consensus-style yen long at almost no carry cost.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the BoJ delivers on both 18 December and 22 January and a Gulf settlement cuts LNG prices, the yen's gains against the dollar would outpace the Singapore dollar's, and the cross would fall broadly in line with the dollar-leg consensus. The funding rotation (yen +2.7% against the dollar in the second half of the year versus 1.3% for the Singapore dollar) is the main risk to the tactical long.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: Tactically, the four-week window contains Japanese growth and trade data likely to disappoint, an extreme speculative yen long, and no BoJ decision, so the Singapore dollar's growth and energy advantages edge the score just above the Bullish threshold. Strategically, the weights move towards Guidance and External Balance, and Japan's inflation profile gains relevance. The BoJ's scheduled decisions on 18 December and 22 January then offset the energy and fiscal asymmetries, and the score falls to Neutral.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The 18 December BoJ decision is the inflection. A hike with hawkish guidance would validate the yen side of the strategic stalemate, while a hold would remove it. The 22 January Outlook Report meeting is the second checkpoint.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Treat the tactical Bullish call as small and short-dated, to be reduced into the December BoJ decision rather than carried through it. Strategically, stay flat on the cross and express single-currency views through crosses with clearer asymmetries.

catalysts.event: US midterm elections (window opens for possible US strikes on Iran); Japanese market holiday
catalysts.rationale: A post-election US strike on Iran would lift oil and LNG, hurting the yen through Japan's import bill more than the Singapore dollar and pushing the pair higher. Any accompanying equity sell-off would favour the yen through repatriation. The Tokyo holiday thins liquidity in an already synthetic cross.

The auction tests Japan's fiscal premium after the 10-year fell from 3.135% to 2.770% in October. A weak result with a tail above 3% would revive supply fears, and in this cycle higher JGB yields on supply have weakened the yen. Singapore has no equivalent fiscal test, so any repricing is one-sided for the cross.

catalysts.event: Governor Ueda remarks; US October payrolls
catalysts.rationale: Ueda's first remarks after the hawkish 30 October hold can move December BoJ pricing by 10-15 points. A firm signal would strengthen the yen against the Singapore dollar, whose central bank is silent until January. Payrolls affect both dollar legs, but the yen's higher beta to the dollar dominates the cross.

catalysts.event: BoJ Summary of Opinions for the 30 October meeting (second week of November)
catalysts.rationale: The opinions will show how many members besides Takata favour a near-term hike. Three or more would lift December pricing towards 85-90%, validating the stretched yen long rather than liquidating it, and would flip both the Guidance and Positioning arguments against the pair at once. It is the single most dangerous event for the tactical long.

catalysts.event: Japan Q3 GDP, first preliminary estimate
catalysts.rationale: The JCER consensus is only +0.08% annualised, and the yen dossier puts a negative print at 40%. A contraction would strengthen the case for waiting on the Board and trim December pricing, widening the growth gap against Singapore's 5.4% and lifting the cross.

October will capture JKM's 27% monthly rise and the start of winter LNG buying, and the yen dossier expects a deficit of JPY0.8-1.2tn against September's JPY0.54tn. That would confirm the energy asymmetry that is the largest structural support for the pair.

catalysts.event: Singapore October non-oil domestic exports (week 3 of November)
catalysts.rationale: September NODX rose 68.4% on a 107.6% jump in electronics. A print above +40% would confirm the export surplus behind Factor 5, while a drop below +20% would be the first sign the AI export cycle is turning. Band management absorbs most of the effect on USD/SGD, so the pair impact is small and comes through the growth gap.

Tokyo's 2.6% ex-fresh-food print points to a national core reading of 2.3-2.5%, up from 2.1%. A 2.4% or higher print would cement December BoJ pricing and strengthen the yen against a Singapore dollar whose core inflation, at 2.0%, argues for an unchanged band.

catalysts.event: Singapore October CPI and MAS core inflation (week 4 of November)
catalysts.rationale: A core print of 1.8% or lower would push the S$NEER towards the band centre and weaken the Singapore dollar against all currencies, including the yen. A print of 2.3% or higher would revive tightening expectations for the January statement. It is the only Singapore data point in the window that can move policy expectations.

catalysts.event: Ministry of Finance monthly intervention data
catalysts.rationale: Shows whether any yen buying took place in November. A non-zero figure would raise the credibility of the yen's ceiling against the dollar, which also limits how far the yen can fall against the Singapore dollar in a dollar-strength episode.

A Fed hike to 4.00-4.25% would lift SORA partly through the forward market and tend to weaken the higher-beta yen more than the band-managed Singapore dollar. But it lands nine days before the BoJ, which can reverse the effect, and near the intervention line it would draw a Japanese policy response.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting
catalysts.rationale: About 75% priced for a hike to 1.50%, which would flip the short-rate gap from about +5bp to about -20bp in the yen's favour. Hawkish guidance would favour the yen, while a hold would be the largest pair-positive event in the horizon. MAS has no verified decision on file to offset it.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 draft budget compilation (late December)
catalysts.rationale: The first budget to quantify the food tax cut and cash payments. Higher JGB supply as the BoJ tapers its purchases has weakened rather than strengthened the yen in this cycle. Singapore has no comparable fiscal event before its February budget, which is expected to stay in surplus.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: A projection round, which moves the pair harder than a bare statement. Core CPI forecasts above 2% through FY2027 and a signal for a further hike would extend the yen's policy momentum. The MAS January statement is expected around this time, but no verified date is on file.

Repatriation and hedge-ratio adjustments by Japanese institutions have historically supported the yen in late February and March, and hedged US Treasury yields below JGB yields strengthen the incentive this year. Japan's large direct-investment stock in Singapore makes Singapore-dollar assets part of that repatriation pool.

assumptions: Price series: daily open, high, low and close for SGD/JPY, 130 weekday sessions from 2026-05-04 to 2026-10-30; spot 123.26702 at the 30 October close. The valuation date is 1 November 2026, a Sunday, so the two-day gap spans a weekend and no trading session is missing. Every level, pip distance and percentage in the report is measured against that close.

Moving averages and zones are computed over the full history of 4,920 weekday sessions from 2007-12-24 to 2026-10-30 (1,011 weekly and 502 monthly bars), not just the 130 sessions shown. The 50-, 100- and 200-day figures are simple averages of trading-day closes; the 200-week is a simple average of weekly closes. Realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days, and ATR(14) is 56 pips.

Zone shortfall: only one resistance zone and eleven support zones met the two-touch threshold. Resistance above spot is therefore supplemented with the 50-, 100- and 200-day averages, October and September swing highs, the 125.00 round number and the 52-week highs, all labelled as uncomputed.

Implied correlation: the 60-day and 20-day correlations between USD/JPY and USD/SGD (about 0.66 and 0.25) are backed out of the realised volatilities of the cross and the two dollar legs. They are realised-based estimates, not option-implied.

Synthetic forwards combine ING's indicative USD/SGD points of 12 October, applied to the 30 October close, with USD/JPY forwards from the CME yen futures roll of 29 October. They are indicative, mixed in vintage and source, and the one-month tenor is noisy. They are presented as a forward built from the two dollar legs, not as a quoted SGD/JPY forward.
Pair-level research: web research found no bank research forecast for SGD/JPY. Model and retail projections are cited for context only.

The Singapore dollar has no policy rate and no 10-year series in the verified rates data. Three-month compounded SORA (1.297%, 30 October) is used as its short rate, and the SGS 10-year close of 2.24% (30 October) comes from the Singapore dossier.

The verified JPY 10-year figure of 3.05% is a monthly reading as of 1 September and is not quoted as a live level. The 30 October JGB 10-year close of 2.770% from the yen dossier is used for the bilateral long-end comparison.

No MAS decision date is on file for 1 November 2026 to 1 March 2027. The January MAS statement is referred to as expected, never as dated. The only verified policy decisions in the window are the Bank of Japan's on 18 December 2026 and 22 January 2027, the latter with an Outlook Report.

No implied volatility and no forward funding differential exist for SGD/JPY, because the Singapore dollar has no listed option or future. Pair implied volatility and the carry-to-vol ratio are left null, and the policy-rate gap is not presented as forward-implied carry. CFTC percentiles are not provided in the report and are left null.
No bank research forecast for SGD/JPY was located. The consensus field is left null rather than built from dollar-leg surveys or extrapolation sites.

Singapore dollar positioning is inferred from the S$NEER estimate (OCBC, 15 October) and MAS reserve changes, because no reportable SGD futures contract exists. Yen positioning is from the CFTC reports for the week to 27 October.
Bilateral goods trade is IMF DOTS 2024 data as supplied. Singapore- and Japan-reported figures differ materially, a mirror-statistics gap, and neither is large enough to create a pair-specific flow.
Probabilities for central bank decisions, Japanese GDP outcomes and geopolitical scenarios are taken from the two dossiers' own estimates unless stated as market pricing.
No factor stance relies on this pair's own recent trading. Price levels, ranges and execution are set in the trade plan.
Scenario probabilities, invalidator probabilities, targets, entries and stops are this analysis's own estimates.

Formatting note: catalysts dated only by a week window in the report were mapped to the Monday of that week (second week of November = 2026-11-09; week 3 = 2026-11-16; week 4 = 2026-11-23; late December = 2026-12-21); the dossier dates were not stated separately, so metadata dossier dates follow the report's 1 November 2026 valuation date.
